items.stem: What 1990 documents set out human rights within the framework of Islamic Sharia?
items.answer: The Cairo Declaration on Human Rights in Islam
items.markingKey: The Cairo Declaration on Human Rights in Islam. Adopted by the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why Amartya Sen rejected the Asian values thesis.
items.answer: Sen argued that Asian traditions (e.g. Ashoka's tolerance, Buddhist and Confucian ideas) contain respect for freedom and that Western traditions were not always liberal; "Asia" is too diverse to have a single set of values.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Sen argued that Asian traditions (e.g. Ashoka's tolerance, Buddhist and Confucian ideas) contain respect for freedom and that Western traditions were not always liberal; "Asia" is too diverse to have a single set of values. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between strong cultural relativism and weak cultural relativism.
items.answer: Strong relativism treats culture as the main source of validity of rights, with universal standards only a check; weak relativism accepts universal rights as the main standard but allows cultural variation in how they are interpreted and implemented (Jack Donnelly).
items.markingKey: Strong relativism treats culture as the main source of validity of rights, with universal standards only a check; weak relativism accepts universal rights as the main standard but allows cultural variation in how they are interpreted and implemented (Jack Donnelly). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"While human rights are universal in nature, they must be considered in the context of a dynamic and evolving process of international norm-setting, bearing in mind the significance of national and regional particularities."
— Bangkok Declaration, Article 8, 1993

With reference to the source, explain how the Bangkok Declaration qualifies universalism.
items.answer: It accepts that rights are universal but argues their application must consider national and regional particularities (culture, history, development), opening space for relativist interpretation.
items.markingKey: It accepts that rights are universal but argues their application must consider national and regional particularities (culture, history, development), opening space for relativist interpretation. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Ingrid writes: "Cultural relativism means that no practice can ever be criticised." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Weak relativism accepts universal minimum standards while allowing variation in interpretation; relativists can still criticise practices such as genocide or slavery.
items.markingKey: Weak relativism accepts universal minimum standards while allowing variation in interpretation; relativists can still criticise practices such as genocide or slavery. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A government argues that criticising its restrictions on media is "Western cultural imperialism". Outline a universalist response and a relativist response.
items.answer: Universalist: freedom of expression (UDHR Art. 19, ICCPR Art. 19) applies to all; the state has ratified the ICCPR; local journalists themselves demand it. Relativist: values of social harmony and community may justify different balances; external pressure ignores local context. 2 marks each.
items.markingKey: Universalist: freedom of expression (UDHR Art. 19, ICCPR Art. 19) applies to all; the state has ratified the ICCPR; local journalists themselves demand it. Relativist: values of social harmony and community may justify different balances; external pressure ignores local context. 2 marks each.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that human rights are a Western concept that cannot be applied universally.
items.answer: Human rights have Western historical roots, but they have been adopted and reshaped by people worldwide, so they are universal in aspiration and contested in interpretation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: UDHR drafted in a Western-dominated UN; individualism; used selectively by Western powers. Arguments against: non-Western drafters and traditions; Vienna 1993 reaffirmation; local movements demand rights (Sudan, Iran's "Woman, Life, Freedom"). Supported judgement: Human rights have Western historical roots, but they have been adopted and reshaped by people worldwide, so they are universal in aspiration and contested in interpretation.

items.stem: Using two contrasting examples, evaluate the extent to which human rights can be both universal and culturally sensitive.
items.answer: Use e.g. FGM campaigns led locally, Indigenous rights, face-veil bans, LGBTQ+ rights in Uganda; discuss weak relativism, overlapping consensus and local ownership; judge.
items.markingKey: Use e.g. FGM campaigns led locally, Indigenous rights, face-veil bans, LGBTQ+ rights in Uganda; discuss weak relativism, overlapping consensus and local ownership; judge.

items.stem: Explain why some states use cultural relativism to reject international human rights criticism.
items.answer: Relativist arguments allow governments to present criticism as Western interference in their culture and sovereignty, shielding practices such as restrictions on speech, LGBTQ+ rights or women's rights from external pressure.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Relativist arguments allow governments to present criticism as Western interference in their culture and sovereignty, shielding practices such as restrictions on speech, LGBTQ+ rights or women's rights from external pressure. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between weak cultural relativism and strong cultural relativism.
items.answer: Strong relativism treats culture as the main source of validity of rights, with universal standards only a check; weak relativism accepts universal rights as the main standard but allows cultural variation in how they are interpreted and implemented (Jack Donnelly).
items.markingKey: Strong relativism treats culture as the main source of validity of rights, with universal standards only a check; weak relativism accepts universal rights as the main standard but allows cultural variation in how they are interpreted and implemented (Jack Donnelly). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using Donnelly's distinction, classify this position: "Everyone has a right to family life, but what counts as a family can vary between societies." Explain.
items.answer: Weak cultural relativism – the universal right is accepted, but its interpretation and implementation vary across cultures.
items.markingKey: Weak cultural relativism – the universal right is accepted, but its interpretation and implementation vary across cultures.

items.stem: Which of the following wrote A Theory of Justice (1971)?
items.answer: John Rawls
items.markingKey: C. Rawls proposed justice as fairness.

items.stem: Briefly explain why Nozick argued that redistributive taxation can be unjust.
items.answer: If people acquired their holdings justly (through fair acquisition and voluntary transfer), taking part of them by taxation violates their rights; Nozick compared taxation of earnings to forced labour.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If people acquired their holdings justly (through fair acquisition and voluntary transfer), taking part of them by taxation violates their rights; Nozick compared taxation of earnings to forced labour. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that utilitarians only care about the happiness of the rich. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Utilitarianism counts each person's happiness equally; because of diminishing marginal utility, it often supports redistribution to the poor.
items.markingKey: Utilitarianism counts each person's happiness equally; because of diminishing marginal utility, it often supports redistribution to the poor. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using Estonia's flat income tax as an example, explain libertarian ideas in policy.
items.answer: Estonia introduced a flat income tax in 1994 and is often praised by free-market advocates for its simple, low-tax system. it reflects a preference for limited redistribution and individual economic freedom
items.markingKey: Context (Estonia introduced a flat income tax in 1994 and is often praised by free-market advocates for its simple, low-tax system.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: it reflects a preference for limited redistribution and individual economic freedom – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to libertarian ideas in policy.

items.stem: Using Nordic welfare states as an example, explain social justice and redistribution.
items.answer: Countries such as Denmark and Norway combine high taxation with universal health care, education and social security, and have low Gini coefficients. they illustrate a Rawlsian-style commitment to reducing inequality through redistribution while maintaining market economies
items.markingKey: Context (Countries such as Denmark and Norway combine high taxation with universal health care, education and social security, and have low Gini coefficients.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: they illustrate a Rawlsian-style commitment to reducing inequality through redistribution while maintaining market economies – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to social justice and redistribution.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Behind the veil, none of us knows whether we will be born in Oslo or in a refugee camp. What rules would we choose then?"
— Lecture on global justice, 2022 (adapted)

With reference to the source, explain how Rawls's veil of ignorance can be applied to global politics.
items.answer: If people did not know their nationality or circumstances, they would choose global principles protecting the least advantaged (e.g. refugees), supporting cosmopolitan duties – though Rawls himself limited the difference principle to domestic societies.
items.markingKey: If people did not know their nationality or circumstances, they would choose global principles protecting the least advantaged (e.g. refugees), supporting cosmopolitan duties – though Rawls himself limited the difference principle to domestic societies. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Which of the following philosophers wrote that the "greatest happiness of the greatest number" is the measure of right and wrong?
items.answer: Jeremy Bentham
items.markingKey: D. Bentham, A Fragment on Government (1776).

items.stem: Identify the theory of justice reflected in each statement: (a) "Taxing my wages to fund welfare is theft", (b) "Inequality is acceptable only if it improves the lot of the poorest", (c) "Choose the policy that produces the most happiness overall".
items.answer: (a) libertarianism (Nozick); (b) Rawls's difference principle; (c) utilitarianism. 1 mark each.
items.markingKey: (a) libertarianism (Nozick); (b) Rawls's difference principle; (c) utilitarianism. 1 mark each.

items.stem: "Justice requires the redistribution of wealth from rich to poor countries." Using one theoretical perspective and relevant case studies, discuss this view.
items.answer: There are strong moral arguments for global redistribution, especially to remedy historical injustice, but disagreement over duties and effectiveness limits consensus.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Singer's duty to aid; historical injustice (colonialism); global inequality extreme. Arguments against: Nozick: no duty beyond respecting rights; aid effectiveness concerns (Moyo); state sovereignty and national responsibility. Supported judgement: There are strong moral arguments for global redistribution, especially to remedy historical injustice, but disagreement over duties and effectiveness limits consensus. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "UNDRIP"?
options: Nozick's theory that a distribution is just if holdings were acquired and transferred justly, whatever the resulting pattern
A theory, associated with Robert Nozick, that prioritises individual liberty and property rights and limits the state to protecting them
The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007), which recognises Indigenous peoples' rights to self-determination, land and free, prior and informed consent
Rights that protect members of national, ethnic, religious or linguistic minorities, including the right to enjoy their culture, religion and language (ICCPR Art. 27)
items.answer: The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007), which recognises Indigenous peoples' rights to self-determination, land and free, prior and informed consent
items.markingKey: C. "UNDRIP" is the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007), which recognises Indigenous peoples' rights to self-determination, land and free, prior and informed consent.

items.stem: Explain why women's rights can be described as both universal and contested.
items.answer: CEDAW is ratified by nearly all states, but reservations, customary and religious laws, and political backlash (e.g. Taliban restrictions, abortion debates) mean the meaning and priority of women's rights remain contested.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: CEDAW is ratified by nearly all states, but reservations, customary and religious laws, and political backlash (e.g. Taliban restrictions, abortion debates) mean the meaning and priority of women's rights remain contested. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Sofia writes: "The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples is a binding treaty that Indigenous peoples can enforce in international courts." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: UNDRIP is a non-binding General Assembly declaration; some of its provisions reflect binding law (e.g. ILO Convention 169, regional court rulings), and some states have incorporated it domestically (e.g. Canada's 2021 UNDRIP Act).
items.markingKey: UNDRIP is a non-binding General Assembly declaration; some of its provisions reflect binding law (e.g. ILO Convention 169, regional court rulings), and some states have incorporated it domestically (e.g. Canada's 2021 UNDRIP Act). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A mining company plans an open-pit mine on land claimed by an Indigenous community. Explain two rights the community could invoke and one argument the government might make.
items.answer: Rights: collective land rights and FPIC (UNDRIP Arts. 26 and 32; ILO 169); cultural rights (ICCPR Art. 27); right to a healthy environment. Government: national development, jobs and revenue; state ownership of subsoil resources. 2+2 marks.
items.markingKey: Rights: collective land rights and FPIC (UNDRIP Arts. 26 and 32; ILO 169); cultural rights (ICCPR Art. 27); right to a healthy environment. Government: national development, jobs and revenue; state ownership of subsoil resources. 2+2 marks.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Consultation is not consent. They came, they explained the dam, and then they built it."
— Statement by an Indigenous leader in the Brazilian Amazon, 2015 (adapted)

With reference to the source, explain the principle of free, prior and informed consent.
items.answer: FPIC requires that Indigenous peoples can say no, not just be informed; the source criticises a process where consultation occurred but consent was not obtained (e.g. Belo Monte dam).
items.markingKey: FPIC requires that Indigenous peoples can say no, not just be informed; the source criticises a process where consultation occurred but consent was not obtained (e.g. Belo Monte dam). Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The rights of Indigenous peoples are now well protected by international law."
items.answer: International law recognises Indigenous rights more than ever, but protection on the ground remains weak.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: UNDRIP 2007, ILO 169; regional court rulings (Awas Tingni, Saramaka); Canada's UNDRIP Act. Arguments against: non-binding declaration; land conflicts and violence against defenders; FPIC often ignored. Supported judgement: International law recognises Indigenous rights more than ever, but protection on the ground remains weak.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the rights of Indigenous peoples are often in conflict with development projects.
items.answer: Mining, dams, oil and agribusiness frequently target Indigenous lands rich in resources; states and companies prioritise national growth and revenue, while Indigenous communities claim collective land rights and FPIC (e.g. Standing Rock, Belo Monte dam).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Mining, dams, oil and agribusiness frequently target Indigenous lands rich in resources; states and companies prioritise national growth and revenue, while Indigenous communities claim collective land rights and FPIC (e.g. Standing Rock, Belo Monte dam). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Using Standing Rock protests (2016–2017) as an example, explain Indigenous rights versus development.
items.answer: The Standing Rock Sioux and allies protested against the Dakota Access Pipeline near their water source and sacred sites; the pipeline was completed in 2017. the case shows conflict over free, prior and informed consent and the power imbalance between Indigenous communities, the state and energy companies
items.markingKey: Context (The Standing Rock Sioux and allies protested against the Dakota Access Pipeline near their water source and sacred sites; the pipeline was completed in 2017.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the case shows conflict over free, prior and informed consent and the power imbalance between Indigenous communities, the state and energy companies – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to Indigenous rights versus development.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Responding to criticism by pointing to the critic's own failings rather than addressing the charge"?
items.answer: whataboutism
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of whataboutism.

items.stem: Explain why sanctions on whole economies can harm human rights.
items.answer: Broad sanctions can reduce access to food, medicine and jobs for ordinary people while elites adapt (e.g. Iraq in the 1990s), so they may violate socio-economic rights even when aimed at rights violators.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Broad sanctions can reduce access to food, medicine and jobs for ordinary people while elites adapt (e.g. Iraq in the 1990s), so they may violate socio-economic rights even when aimed at rights violators. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Because human rights are sometimes used politically, they have no value." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Selective use reveals hypocrisy but does not invalidate the norms themselves; victims and NGOs use them regardless of states' motives.
items.markingKey: Selective use reveals hypocrisy but does not invalidate the norms themselves; victims and NGOs use them regardless of states' motives. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which sanctions over Xinjiang shows rights in foreign policy.
items.answer: In 2021 the EU, UK, US and Canada sanctioned Chinese officials over Uyghur detention; China retaliated by sanctioning MEPs and academics, and the EU–China investment agreement was frozen. human rights were used as a foreign policy tool, provoking counter-sanctions and showing the costs of rights diplomacy
items.markingKey: Context (In 2021 the EU, UK, US and Canada sanctioned Chinese officials over Uyghur detention; China retaliated by sanctioning MEPs and academics, and the EU–China investment agreement was frozen.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: human rights were used as a foreign policy tool, provoking counter-sanctions and showing the costs of rights diplomacy – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to rights in foreign policy.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that sanctions are an effective way to improve human rights.
items.answer: Sanctions rarely change regimes' behaviour alone; they are most effective when multilateral, targeted and combined with diplomacy and domestic pressure.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: South Africa apartheid sanctions; targeted sanctions stigmatise abusers. Arguments against: Iran, North Korea, Cuba unchanged; humanitarian harm (Iraq 1990s); rally-round-the-flag effects. Supported judgement: Sanctions rarely change regimes' behaviour alone; they are most effective when multilateral, targeted and combined with diplomacy and domestic pressure.

items.stem: Briefly explain why human rights criticism is often accused of being selective.
items.answer: Powerful states tend to criticise adversaries (e.g. Iran, Russia) while muting criticism of allies or trade partners (e.g. Saudi Arabia, Egypt), which suggests strategic interests shape human rights diplomacy.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Powerful states tend to criticise adversaries (e.g. Iran, Russia) while muting criticism of allies or trade partners (e.g. Saudi Arabia, Egypt), which suggests strategic interests shape human rights diplomacy. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Targeted sanctions are our way of saying: you personally will not shop in Paris or bank in London while you torture people at home."
— EU parliamentarian, 2021 (adapted)

Explain, with reference to the source, the purpose of targeted human rights sanctions.
items.answer: They impose personal costs (travel bans, asset freezes) on individuals responsible for abuses, stigmatising them while avoiding harm to the general population.
items.markingKey: They impose personal costs (travel bans, asset freezes) on individuals responsible for abuses, stigmatising them while avoiding harm to the general population. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The imposition of one culture's values, practices or institutions on other societies, often by more powerful states"?
items.answer: cultural imperialism
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of cultural imperialism.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The theory, associated with Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill, that the right action is the one that produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number"?
items.answer: utilitarianism
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of utilitarianism.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "intersectionality".
items.answer: The idea, developed by Kimberlé Crenshaw, that forms of discrimination such as race, gender and class overlap and compound each other
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the idea, developed by Kimberlé Crenshaw, that forms of discrimination such as race, gender and class overlap and compound each other. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why states with poor human rights records seek membership of the Human Rights Council.
items.answer: Membership allows them to influence resolutions, block scrutiny of themselves and allies, and gain legitimacy; this has led to criticism of the Council's credibility.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Membership allows them to influence resolutions, block scrutiny of themselves and allies, and gain legitimacy; this has led to criticism of the Council's credibility. items.stem: Distinguish between retributive justice and distributive justice.
items.answer: Distributive justice concerns the fair allocation of resources and opportunities in society; retributive justice concerns fair punishment for wrongdoing, such as trials for war crimes.
items.markingKey: Distributive justice concerns the fair allocation of resources and opportunities in society; retributive justice concerns fair punishment for wrongdoing, such as trials for war crimes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Minority rights mean minorities can ignore national laws." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Minority rights protect culture, religion and language within the framework of human rights and national law; they do not exempt minorities from general laws.
items.markingKey: Minority rights protect culture, religion and language within the framework of human rights and national law; they do not exempt minorities from general laws. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between comprehensive sanctions and targeted sanctions.
items.answer: Targeted sanctions freeze assets or ban travel of specific individuals or entities responsible for abuses; comprehensive sanctions restrict trade with an entire country, affecting the whole population.
items.markingKey: Targeted sanctions freeze assets or ban travel of specific individuals or entities responsible for abuses; comprehensive sanctions restrict trade with an entire country, affecting the whole population. items.stem: Distinguish between cultural relativism and universalism.
items.answer: Universalism holds that the same human rights apply to everyone everywhere because of shared humanity; cultural relativism holds that rights and values derive from cultural contexts and that outsiders should not impose their standards.
items.markingKey: Universalism holds that the same human rights apply to everyone everywhere because of shared humanity; cultural relativism holds that rights and values derive from cultural contexts and that outsiders should not impose their standards. items.stem: Isabel writes: "Rawls believed that all inequality is unjust." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Rawls accepted inequalities if they benefit the least advantaged and are attached to positions open to all under fair equality of opportunity.
items.markingKey: Rawls accepted inequalities if they benefit the least advantaged and are attached to positions open to all under fair equality of opportunity. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

Read the source below.

"Our grandmothers suffered in silence because they were told it was tradition. We are also part of our culture, and we say no."
— Statement by a young activist against child marriage in West Africa, 2021 (adapted)

Explain, with reference to the source, a criticism of cultural relativism.
items.answer: Cultures are internally contested; those affected may reject harmful traditions, so relativism can privilege elders' or elites' interpretations over the rights of vulnerable members.

items.stem: Apply two theories of justice to a contemporary global issue and evaluate which offers the more convincing analysis.

items.markingKey: E.g. climate finance, refugees, vaccine distribution, global taxation; apply Rawls, utilitarianism, Nozick or Sen; compare implications and weaknesses.

items.stem:

"Our laws reflect our faith and our families. Foreign governments that tie aid to so-called sexual rights are practising a new colonialism."

Identify the argument in the source and explain one counter-argument.
items.answer: Cultural relativist/sovereignty argument that LGBTQ+ rights are foreign impositions; counter: non-discrimination is part of universal rights (ICCPR Art. 26, Toonen) and LGBTQ+ people exist within every culture.

items.stem: "Human rights are used mainly as a tool of foreign policy by powerful states." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Powerful states often instrumentalise rights, but rights also have independent force through law, NGOs and victims, so they are not merely tools.

items.stem: Chloé writes: "Because human rights are sometimes used politically, they have no value." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Selective use reveals hypocrisy but does not invalidate the norms themselves; victims and NGOs use them regardless of states' motives.
items.markingKey: Selective use reveals hypocrisy but does not invalidate the norms themselves; victims and NGOs use them regardless of states' motives. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "The idea of universal human rights was rejected by all non-Western states at Vienna in 1993." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: At Vienna 171 states, including those that signed the Bangkok Declaration, affirmed that rights are universal, while noting national and regional particularities.
items.markingKey: At Vienna 171 states, including those that signed the Bangkok Declaration, affirmed that rights are universal, while noting national and regional particularities. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between Rawls's theory of justice and Nozick's theory of justice.
items.answer: Rawls judges justice by the pattern of distribution, permitting redistribution to benefit the least advantaged; Nozick judges justice by the history of how holdings were acquired, rejecting patterned redistribution.
items.markingKey: Rawls judges justice by the pattern of distribution, permitting redistribution to benefit the least advantaged; Nozick judges justice by the history of how holdings were acquired, rejecting patterned redistribution. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between substantive equality and formal equality.
items.answer: Formal equality means equal treatment in law; substantive equality aims for equal outcomes in practice, which may require special measures such as quotas or affirmative action.
items.markingKey: Formal equality means equal treatment in law; substantive equality aims for equal outcomes in practice, which may require special measures such as quotas or affirmative action. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that because human rights are sometimes used politically, they have no value. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Selective use reveals hypocrisy but does not invalidate the norms themselves; victims and NGOs use them regardless of states' motives.
items.markingKey: Selective use reveals hypocrisy but does not invalidate the norms themselves; victims and NGOs use them regardless of states' motives. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between strong cultural relativism and weak cultural relativism.
items.answer: Strong relativism treats culture as the main source of validity of rights, with universal standards only a check; weak relativism accepts universal rights as the main standard but allows cultural variation in how they are interpreted and implemented (Jack Donnelly).
items.markingKey: Strong relativism treats culture as the main source of validity of rights, with universal standards only a check; weak relativism accepts universal rights as the main standard but allows cultural variation in how they are interpreted and implemented (Jack Donnelly). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly describe global vaccine distribution during COVID-19 and explain what it reveals about theories of justice applied globally.
items.answer: High-income countries vaccinated most adults by late 2021, while low-income countries had vaccinated only a few per cent; WHO and COVAX called for fairer allocation. a Rawlsian or utilitarian view would favour prioritising the most vulnerable worldwide, whereas nationalist positions prioritised citizens
items.markingKey: Context (High-income countries vaccinated most adults by late 2021, while low-income countries had vaccinated only a few per cent; WHO and COVAX called for fairer allocation.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: a Rawlsian or utilitarian view would favour prioritising the most vulnerable worldwide, whereas nationalist positions prioritised citizens – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to theories of justice applied globally.

items.stem: Using the Rohingya in Myanmar as an example, explain the rights of minorities.
items.answer: The Rohingya were largely stripped of citizenship by Myanmar's 1982 Citizenship Law and faced military "clearance operations" in 2017; The Gambia brought a genocide case at the ICJ in 2019. denial of citizenship made a minority especially vulnerable, and international legal action has tried to provide accountability
items.markingKey: Context (The Rohingya were largely stripped of citizenship by Myanmar's 1982 Citizenship Law and faced military "clearance operations" in 2017; The Gambia brought a genocide case at the ICJ in 2019.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: denial of citizenship made a minority especially vulnerable, and international legal action has tried to provide accountability – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the rights of minorities.

items.stem: Using the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar as an example, explain the politics of rights criticism.
items.answer: Rights groups highlighted migrant worker deaths and the kafala system; Qatar introduced some labour reforms but rejected Western criticism as hypocritical. scrutiny produced some reforms but also accusations of Western double standards
items.markingKey: Context (Rights groups highlighted migrant worker deaths and the kafala system; Qatar introduced some labour reforms but rejected Western criticism as hypocritical.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: scrutiny produced some reforms but also accusations of Western double standards – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the politics of rights criticism.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Asian values debate in the 1990s and explain what it reveals about the relativist challenge to universal rights.
items.answer: Lee Kuan Yew and Mahathir Mohamad argued that Asian societies valued order and community; Kim Dae-jung of South Korea responded that democracy was compatible with Asian traditions. the debate showed that claims about "culture" are contested within Asia itself
items.markingKey: Context (Lee Kuan Yew and Mahathir Mohamad argued that Asian societies valued order and community; Kim Dae-jung of South Korea responded that democracy was compatible with Asian traditions.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the debate showed that claims about "culture" are contested within Asia itself – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the relativist challenge to universal rights.

items.stem: With reference to Nordic welfare states, explain how it illustrates social justice and redistribution.
items.answer: Countries such as Denmark and Norway combine high taxation with universal health care, education and social security, and have low Gini coefficients. they illustrate a Rawlsian-style commitment to reducing inequality through redistribution while maintaining market economies
items.markingKey: Context (Countries such as Denmark and Norway combine high taxation with universal health care, education and social security, and have low Gini coefficients.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: they illustrate a Rawlsian-style commitment to reducing inequality through redistribution while maintaining market economies – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to social justice and redistribution.

items.stem: Using the concept of intersectionality, explain why Indigenous women may face particular rights violations.
items.answer: They may face combined discrimination based on gender, ethnicity and poverty – e.g. high rates of violence (Canada's inquiry into missing and murdered Indigenous women and girls, 2019) and poor access to services – that neither gender-based nor ethnicity-based analysis alone captures.
items.markingKey: They may face combined discrimination based on gender, ethnicity and poverty – e.g. high rates of violence (Canada's inquiry into missing and murdered Indigenous women and girls, 2019) and poor access to services – that neither gender-based nor ethnicity-based analysis alone captures.

items.stem: A state imposes sanctions on a rival for human rights abuses but continues arms sales to an ally accused of similar abuses. Explain two consequences of this inconsistency.
items.answer: It undermines the credibility of the sanctioning state's human rights claims; it allows the target to dismiss criticism as political (whataboutism); it weakens the universal norm. 2 marks each.
items.markingKey: It undermines the credibility of the sanctioning state's human rights claims; it allows the target to dismiss criticism as political (whataboutism); it weakens the universal norm. 2 marks each.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that human rights are a Western concept that cannot be applied universally.
items.answer: Human rights have Western historical roots, but they have been adopted and reshaped by people worldwide, so they are universal in aspiration and contested in interpretation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: UDHR drafted in a Western-dominated UN; individualism; used selectively by Western powers. Arguments against: non-Western drafters and traditions; Vienna 1993 reaffirmation; local movements demand rights (Sudan, Iran's "Woman, Life, Freedom"). Supported judgement: Human rights have Western historical roots, but they have been adopted and reshaped by people worldwide, so they are universal in aspiration and contested in interpretation.

items.stem: "Rawls's theory provides the most convincing account of justice." Discuss.
items.answer: Rawls offers a powerful framework balancing liberty and equality, but it is contested and needs extending to global and capability-based concerns.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: fair procedure (veil of ignorance); protects the least advantaged; combines liberty and equality. Arguments against: Nozick: ignores rights to property and history; utilitarians: welfare maximisation; Sen: focus on capabilities and real lives; cosmopolitan critics: limited to nation-states. Supported judgement: Rawls offers a powerful framework balancing liberty and equality, but it is contested and needs extending to global and capability-based concerns. Markbands: Markbands (scaled to the marks available, five bands): top band – sharply focused, accurate knowledge of concepts, theories and specific examples, well-developed counter-claims and a clear, well-supported judgement; upper-middle – focused, relevant examples, counter-claims addressed, reasoned conclusion; middle – mostly focused, some examples and counter-claims, conclusion stated; lower – limited, mainly descriptive knowledge with little evaluation; bottom – minimal relevant knowledge, no evaluation.

items.stem: Analyse why the rights of one group you have studied remain contested, and evaluate the effectiveness of efforts to protect them.
items.answer: Choose e.g. Rohingya, Uyghurs, Indigenous peoples in Brazil, LGBTQ+ people in Uganda, Afghan women; identify sources of contestation (sovereignty, culture, economics) and evaluate protection mechanisms.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that the selective use of human rights in foreign policy undermines their legitimacy.
items.answer: Discuss cases (Khashoggi, Xinjiang, Qatar, Russia suspension, Gaza responses); distinguish norm legitimacy from state credibility; judge.
